lead: This unit gives you the words the rest of the subject uses: the goals a secure system must meet, the attacks that break them, and the ways attackers get in. After it you can look at a news report or a network diagram and say which goal broke, which class of attack it was, and which defence layer should have stopped it.
about: Unit 1 builds the vocabulary the later units assume. Chapter 1.1 states the security goals: confidentiality, integrity and availability, plus the extra goals of authentication and non-repudiation. Chapter 1.2 turns those goals into the standard language of attacks, services and mechanisms, so you can say what a system needs before you name a cipher. Chapter 1.3 connects threats, vulnerabilities and attack vectors, and shows how risk is scored in money. Chapters 1.4 to 1.7 then walk through the attacks themselves: network attacks such as DoS, DDoS, MITM, replay and port scanning; malware; social engineering and phishing; and botnets with remote access attacks. Every later unit supplies the fixes — number theory in Unit 2, ciphers in Units 3 and 4, protocols in Unit 5, firewalls and intrusion detection in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Every security requirement is one of three promises: keep the data secret, keep the data correct, keep the service reachable.
chapters.depth: Define confidentiality, integrity and availability with one everyday Indian example each (a UPI payment, a mark sheet, an IRCTC booking page). Add the extra goals some syllabi list: authentication, accountability and non-repudiation. Show the negation set some syllabi call DAD — disclosure, alteration, destruction. Show that controls trade off against each other: encryption protects confidentiality but costs CPU, so heavy encryption can lower availability. Some syllabi place a trust and threat model here: who you trust, what they can do, what you assume about them. Some syllabi also build a confidentiality determination matrix, an asset-by-data-class table that assigns public, internal or restricted to each asset; show one small table. State availability as an uptime percentage over a stated period.

figure.title: One message, three promises

nodes.label: Confidentiality
nodes.note: only the two parties read it

figure.aria: One message in transit is shown branching into the three goals, with the failure that breaks each goal written on the branch.

chapters.example: A college result portal runs continuously for 30 days, which is 30 × 24 × 60 = 43200 minutes. (a) The portal was down for 108 minutes, so availability = (43200 − 108) ÷ 43200 = 99.75%. (b) A student edits his own marks row in the database: integrity is broken. (c) A mark sheet PDF is readable by anyone who has the link, with no login: confidentiality is broken. (d) Only exam-cell staff can publish results, and each publish is signed: this gives authentication and non-repudiation. Name the goal broken in each case.
chapters.trap: Writing 'security means confidentiality'. Most marks come from naming the goal that a stated incident broke: a crash is availability, a silent edit is integrity, a leak is confidentiality. Availability is a percentage over a stated period, not the sentence 'the server is up'.
chapters.leave: Encryption algorithms, MACs and digital signatures belong to Units 3 and 4. Access control models, firewalls and intrusion detection belong to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Attacks are classified, services are what you promise, mechanisms are how you deliver the promise.
chapters.depth: Passive versus active attacks. The four attack classes: interruption, interception, modification, fabrication. The X.800 list of services: authentication, access control, data confidentiality, data integrity, non-repudiation, availability. The mechanisms: encipherment, digital signature, access control, data integrity, authentication exchange, traffic padding, routing control, notarization. Some syllabi call mechanisms 'security controls' and split them into preventive, detective and corrective. Practise the three-column mapping attack → service → mechanism on paper, since that is how the question is usually set.

figure.title: Attack, service, mechanism
figure.aria: A four-step chain runs left to right from threat to attack to the service that must survive it to the mechanism that provides that service.

chapters.example: An employee downloads the salary file from the office server. Classify each event as attack class, service needed and mechanism. (a) A switch mirror copies the packets but the file body is unreadable: passive interception, confidentiality, encipherment. (b) The amount field changes in transit from ₹45,000 to ₹95,000: active modification, data integrity, MAC or digital signature. (c) The file server stops answering for 3 hours: active interruption, availability, redundancy plus rate limiting. (d) The sender later denies sending the file: non-repudiation, digital signature.
chapters.trap: Mixing the three columns: writing 'encryption' when the question asks for a service, or 'confidentiality' when it asks for a mechanism. Read whether the question wants what breaks, what is promised, or how it is done.
chapters.prereq: 1.1, because each service in this chapter protects one of the goals defined there.
chapters.leave: The working details of ciphers, MACs and signatures are in Units 3 and 4. Protocol-level services such as TLS, IPsec and Kerberos are in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A threat needs a vulnerability to become a loss; risk is the expected size of that loss.
chapters.depth: Define asset, threat, threat agent, vulnerability, exposure, risk, attack vector and attack surface. Threat catalog and vulnerability catalog as lists an organisation keeps and updates; public reference lists are CVE for individual vulnerabilities, CWE for weakness classes and CVSS for a 0 to 10 severity score. Threat–vulnerability pairs: one row per sentence 'this actor can use this weakness'. Risk = likelihood × impact; annualised loss expectancy = single loss × annual rate. Distinguish attack vector (the path used) from attack surface (everything reachable). Some syllabi present this as compiling observations from organisational risk documents into a fixed table format, with one column per field. Keep the worked example in rupees.

figure.title: From asset to risk, with a control
figure.aria: A downward chain from asset to vulnerability to threat to risk, with a control box that feeds back to the vulnerability to remove it.

chapters.example: A firm has 400 internal web servers. A scan finds 25% of them run an unpatched library with a known remote-code bug. The chance of a successful exploit in a year is estimated at 0.20. One exploit costs ₹50,00,000 in downtime, forensics and fines. (a) Exposed servers = 0.25 × 400 = 100. (b) Annual risk = 0.20 × 50,00,000 = ₹10,00,000. (c) A patch project costs ₹3,00,000 and cuts the chance to 0.04, so the new risk = 0.04 × 50,00,000 = ₹2,00,000. (d) Saving = 10,00,000 − 2,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.
chapters.trap: Calling a vulnerability a threat, or a threat a risk. A threat is who or what can act; a vulnerability is the weakness that lets it work; risk is the expected damage, usually in money or severity score.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the goals that each risk is measured against, and 1.2 for the word 'attack'.
chapters.leave: Risk management policy, audits and security policies in full are in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Most network attacks do one of three things: drown a service, sit in the middle of a conversation, or reuse a captured message.
chapters.depth: DoS versus DDoS, and the three families: volumetric, protocol-level, application-layer. SYN flood and the half-open connection table; reflection and amplification using DNS or NTP. MITM by ARP cache poisoning, DNS spoofing, a rogue Wi-Fi access point, or BGP hijack (one line only). Replay attack and the freshness fix: nonce, timestamp or sequence number. Port scanning types: TCP connect, SYN (half-open), FIN, UDP, and what open, closed and filtered ports look like; name nmap as the common tool and note the legality of scanning. LAN attacks that make MITM possible: ARP poisoning, MAC flooding, DHCP starvation, VLAN hopping.

figure.aria: Client and server talk through an attacker in the middle, and the attacker later resends a captured message with seq = 1000, which the server accepts a second time.

chapters.example: A botnet of 50,000 hosts sends 200 HTTP requests per second each at one web server. (a) Load = 50,000 × 200 = 1,00,00,000 requests per second. The server handles 20,000 per second, so it is 500 times over capacity. (b) With a spoofed source address per request, per-IP rate limiting fails; the fix is upstream scrubbing plus SYN-cookie style handling. (c) A port scan of the same host shows 22, 80 and 443 open, and 3306 filtered, meaning a firewall rule drops packets to 3306.
chapters.trap: Describing DDoS as 'many DoS'. The defence changes: you cannot block one address, so you need upstream filtering, anycast or scrubbing. Also, replay is stopped by freshness, not by encryption alone.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 for passive and active attack classes, and 1.3 for attack vector and attack surface.
chapters.leave: TLS, IPsec, DNSSEC, SSH and BGP security as protocols are in Unit 5. Firewalls, IDS and honeypots are in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Malware is classified by how it spreads and what it needs: a host file, a network, or a user's trust.
chapters.depth: Virus: needs a host file and usually a user action; subtypes boot sector, file infector, macro, polymorphic (changes its own bytes to avoid signatures) and stealth. Worm: spreads by itself over the network and needs no host program; the classic 1988 Morris worm used a mail bug and a list of weak passwords. Trojan: looks useful and hides a payload; payload types include backdoor, rootkit, logic bomb, spyware and ransomware. Lifecycle: delivery, execution, persistence, payload, propagation. Say clearly that a program bug exploited by malware is covered in Unit 6.

figure.aria: A tree with Malware at the root and virus, worm and trojan as branches, showing that a virus needs a host file, a worm spreads alone, and a trojan hides in a useful program.

chapters.example: A worm doubles the number of infected machines every 10 minutes and starts at 1 machine at 09:00. (a) At 09:10 there are 2 infected machines, at 09:20 four, at 09:30 eight. (b) By 10:00 six doubling steps have passed, so 2⁶ = 64 machines. (c) A network of 1,00,000 machines is passed between step 16 (65,536 at 11:40) and step 17 (1,31,072 at 11:50). (d) Because no user action is needed, patching the one bug stops the worm; a virus of the same speed would need 64 users to open the file first.
chapters.trap: Calling every piece of bad software a virus. If it spreads alone over the network it is a worm; if it hides inside a program the user wanted, it is a trojan.
chapters.prereq: 1.3 for vulnerability and exposure, since malware usually enters through an unpatched service.
chapters.leave: Buffer overflows, safe coding, OS hardening and antivirus controls are in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Social engineering attacks the person, so the only defence is a habit plus a technical backstop, not a patch.
chapters.depth: Techniques: pretexting, baiting, tailgating, quid pro quo, and the levers of urgency, authority and fear. Phishing and its variants: spear phishing (targeted), whaling (senior staff), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice call), pharming (traffic redirected without a click), clone phishing (a copy of a real mail with a swapped link). Anatomy of a phishing mail: lookalike domain, spoofed display name, urgent deadline, link to a credential page, request for an OTP. Typosquatting and lookalike characters. Defences at three layers: people (training, a report button), mail (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, one line only) and technology (MFA, password managers, link inspection). Give the red-flag checklist.

figure.title: Anatomy of a phishing attack
figure.aria: A five-step chain runs left to right from reconnaissance to the lure mail to the fake login page to use of the stolen password to money leaving the account.

chapters.example: A phishing campaign sends 10,000 mails. 5% of receivers click the link, 10% of those type their password, and the average loss per taken account is ₹40,000. (a) Clicks = 0.05 × 10,000 = 500. (b) Credentials captured = 0.10 × 500 = 50. (c) Expected loss = 50 × 40,000 = ₹20,00,000. (d) If training halves the click rate and MFA blocks password-only logins, taken accounts fall from 50 to 0, so the loss becomes ₹0 and only the training cost remains.
chapters.trap: Treating phishing as only a mail-filter problem. The answer needs the human layer: urgency, authority, a domain that differs from the real one, and a request for a password or OTP.
chapters.prereq: 1.3 for attack vector, since phishing is an attack vector that bypasses the network entirely.
chapters.leave: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, PGP and S/MIME details are in Unit 5. Password and multi-factor authentication design is also in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A botnet is a rented army of infected machines, and remote access is how the attacker recruits and controls them.
chapters.depth: Bot = a compromised host under remote control; botnet = the set of bots; botmaster (herder); command-and-control channel, centralised (IRC, HTTP) or peer-to-peer; fast flux and domain generation algorithms in one line each. Lifecycle: spread, rally, command, monetise — DDoS-for-hire, spam, credential stuffing, click fraud, crypto mining. Remote access attacks: RDP and SSH brute force, management ports open to the internet, default credentials, web shells, remote access trojans, VPN without MFA. Beacon interval and jitter. Note that detection belongs to Unit 6.

figure.aria: A tree with the botmaster at the top, one command-and-control server below it, and three infected bots that check in every 60 seconds.

chapters.example: A credential-stuffing botnet has 20,000 bots, each trying 50 logins per hour, and 0.1% of attempts succeed. (a) Attempts per hour = 20,000 × 50 = 10,00,000. (b) Successful logins per hour = 0.001 × 10,00,000 = 1000. (c) With a beacon every 60 s, each bot checks in 3600 ÷ 60 = 60 times an hour, so 20,000 × 60 = 12,00,000 beacons per hour reach the C2 server. (d) Blocking the C2 domain stops new commands but leaves the bots infected; rate limiting at the login page plus MFA takes (b) to 0.
chapters.trap: Confusing a bot with a virus. A virus is code that copies itself into files; a bot is a machine already under someone else's control. Also, always name the command-and-control channel — a botnet without one is just malware.
chapters.prereq: 1.4 for DDoS and port scanning, and 1.5 for how the infection arrives.
chapters.leave: SSH, TLS and VPN protocol details are in Unit 5. IDS, honeypots and netflow monitoring are in Unit 6.
